# Research on the Steering Torque Control for Intelligent Vehicles Co-Driving With the Penalty Factor of Human–Machine Intervention

Jian Wu , Qingfeng Kong , Kaiming Yang , Member, IEEE, Yahui Liu , Member, IEEE, Dongpu Cao, Senior Member, IEEE, and Zhenyang Li

**Abstract—In intelligent vehicle cooperative systems, the mismatch in driving characteristics between a human and a machine and the driver misoperation caused by this mismatch result in human–machine conflicts, which significantly affect driving safety. Therefore, an intelligent vehicle human–machine cooperative steering torque control method is proposed herein. To adapt the intelligent system to the varying previewing characteristics of a human, a time-varying previewing driver model is constructed, and a penalty factor for human–machine intervention is designed based on fuzzy rules to assign driving control rights by assessing the driver’s state. Consequently, a human– vehicle–road model with driver preview time and penalty factor as varying parameters is established. Based on gain-scheduling control, a human–machine cooperative steering torque controller is designed to adapt to the varying previewing characteristics of a human and the change in human–machine intervention. The stability and robustness of the entire parameter space are guaranteed by constraining the poles in a certain region. Finally, the proposed human–machine cooperative control scheme demonstrates the effective alleviation of conflicts between the driver and the intelligent driving system.**

**Index Terms—Human–machine cooperation, linear varying parameters, penalty factor, steering assistance torque.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

HE TECHNOLOGY whereby the operation of the vehicle is outside the control of the driver is known as driverless technology. The simple path tracking control utilized in this technology is primarily based on the steering angle loop of the automatic steering system. However, the automatic steering system based on the steering angle loop does not allow the driver to interfere with the steering control, resulting in the driver’s disengagement from the vehicle control and ergonomics problems, such as overdependence and reduced situational awareness [1], [2]. Therefore, scholars proposed the concept of human–machine cooperative driving, which refers to the driving mode in which the driver (human) and intelligent driving system (machine) share the control authority and cooperate to perform vehicle control. Currently, human–machine co-driving is receiving significant attention and will be investigated intensively in the field of intelligent driving [3], [4].

The steering control of human–machine co-driving can be achieved via angle superposition on the steering system; however, this angle superposition mode relies on the steeringby-wire or active front steering system. These two types of steering systems have not been widely adopted, and drivers that use these schemes cannot intuitively feel the steering input of the intelligent driving system, resulting in imperfect human–machine interactions [4]. Additionally, human– machine co-driving can be realized via torque superposition. Steering torque is generated by the intelligent-assisted driving system to guide the driver to drive correctly. The driver and machine share the control authority of the steering system [5]. The steering torque superposition scheme can ensure the final control over the vehicle by the driver without panic caused by the driver’s disengagement from the vehicle control [3]–[5]. During human–machine co-driving, the mismatch in driving characteristics between a human and machine and human error will cause conflicts, which significantly affect driving safety. Therefore, human–machine conflicts must be alleviated to ensure safety.

First, the steering behavior of the driver must be considered in the design of the intelligent driving system; therefore, a driver model that describes the steering behavior of the driver must be developed. Optimal control theory was adopted to model driver behavior [6]. A linear driver model based on multipoint preview was proposed to simulate a driver’s steering behavior by solving a series of linear quadratic problems [7]. A nonlinear driver steering model based on a model predictive control framework was proposed [8]. A multipoint optimal preview model based on road curvature and feedback regarding lane position was proposed [9]. In human–machine co-driving, whereas the change in driver’s previewing characteristics significantly affects steering conflicts and it has not been focused sufficiently in current investigations. Therefore, we herein propose a time-varying previewing driver model based on road curvature, which can describe the behavior of drivers and reduce potential conflicts between drivers and intelligent assistance systems.

Scholars have conducted comprehensive investigations regarding the control strategy design of driving assistance systems. For example, a model-free scheme was introduced by mapping the road error to the driver’s steering moment; however, the scheme does not account for the driver’s behavior [10]. Meanwhile, a linear time-varying model predictive control method based on steering torque input was proposed [11]. Automatic control of lateral motion was achieved via the torque of the steering motor instead of the steering angle. In the human–machine torque superposition scheme, the steering system, steering resistance torque model, and human input as external interference were introduced into the vehicle model, which increased the nonlinearities and uncertainties of the system. In another study, a robust control method of steering torque superposition based on a linear matrix inequality (LMI) algorithm was proposed [12]. In fact, the dynamic interactive control of man–machine cooperation has been investigated extensively. It primarily involves the driver’s behavior, state, and road environment information to coordinate the control of the driver and an intelligent driving system [13]–[15]. To balance between the freedom of operation and vehicle driving safety, a human–machine hybrid input method was adopted for vehicle control, and a human–machine weight was assigned based on the degree of danger [14].

Some scholars believe that the driver’s intention should be considered when designing an assisted driving system [16], [17]. The identification of driver intention can reduce man–machine conflicts and provide a new idea for man–machine cooperative control. Some scholars designed driving weights by assessing drivers’ driving behavior. To avoid human–machine conflicts, a variable weight control algorithm was proposed to predict driver behavior using a two-point predictive driver behavior model [18]. A pseudopower method based on a driving assistance system was proposed to assess the consistency between a human and a machine, after which the functions of the assistance system are switched when appropriate [19]. In the past decade, interactive steering control strategies based on game theory have emerged, which allow the analysis of driver behavior in an intelligent vehicle shared control. To simulate the interaction of steering torque between a driver and an intelligent driving system, a stochastic game control framework based on a shared algorithm was proposed [20]. Ji et al. [21] applied dynamic game theory as the overall framework, regarded the lateral stability of vehicles as a dynamic difference game, and realized the synergy between the active front and rear steering systems. Na and Cole [22], [23] applied noncooperative game theory to simulate the steering interaction between a driver and an AFS. The game strategy proposed in [22] can reasonably represent human–machine interaction during the collision avoidance maneuver; however, the steering-angle-based scheme may cause a complete loss of the driver’s final control [24]. Few existing studies considered the varying previewing characteristics of the driver, which consequently resulted in conflicts caused by human misoperation. Therefore, a penalty factor for human–machine intervention was designed to allocate the control rights of the vehicle based on assessing the driver’s driving behavior. Subsequently, it was used as a linear varying parameter to design a gain-scheduling human–machine cooperative steering torque controller.

The main contributions of this article are summarized as follows.

1) To adapt an intelligent driving system to the varying pre-view characteristics of a human, a model describing a driver’s time-varying previewing characteristics is established using the recursive least squares method based on genetic factors to obtain the relationship between road curvature and preview time.

2) To solve human–machine driving intention conflicts, a penalty factor for human–machine intervention is designed to assign driving control rights by assessing the drivers’ state, which increases or reduces the machine’s intervention, thereby alleviating human– machine conflicts.

3) A gain-scheduling $H _ { \infty }$ human–machine cooperative steering torque controller is designed to adapt to the varying preview characteristics of a human and the change in machine intervention. The D-stability method is used to limit the pole position of vertices in a linear parameter-varying (LPV) system.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. In Section II, the parameter identification of the driver model is presented. Subsequently, the human–vehicle–road model is presented in Section III. Section IV introduces the gainscheduling steering torque control strategies for human– machine co-driving. The simulation results are provided in Section V. Section VI presents the results of an LPV controller based on hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) experiments. Finally, a summary is provided in Section VII.

## II. VARYING PREVIEW DRIVER MODEL AND PARAMETER IDENTIFICATION

## A. Varying Preview Driver Model Based on Steering Torque

Land and Horwood [25] believed that a driver has an optimal preview point on the ahead road. A twopoint previewing driver model is established in [26]. Based on [26] and [27], the lateral deviation $e _ { y p }$ at the driver’s actual previewing point can be calculated by weighting the lateral deviation $e _ { y n }$ at the near point and the lateral deviation $e _ { y f }$ at the far point with λ. This implies that the time-varying characteristics of the driver’s previewing behavior, as shown in Fig. 1, can be described by weighting the deviation at the near and far points.

The time-varying previewing distance and lateral road deviation of the driver can be expressed as follows:

$$
L _ {p} = \lambda L _ {p n} + (1 - \lambda) L _ {p f}\tag{1a}
$$

$$
e _ {y p} = \lambda e _ {y n} + (1 - \lambda) e _ {y f}.\tag{1b}
$$

$L _ { p n }$ and $L _ { p f }$ are the distances of fixed far preview point F and near preview point $N ,$ respectively; $e _ { y n }$ and $e _ { y f }$ are the lateral deviations of preview points N and $F ,$ respectively; and λ is the weighted parameter, which is used to determine the driver’s actual preview point. The previewing time can be expressed as follows:

Fig. 1. Vehicle–road model.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 2. Road scenario. (a) Lateral displacement. (b) Road curvature.

$$
t _ {p} = \frac {L _ {p}}{v _ {x}} = \lambda \frac {L _ {p n}}{v _ {x}} + (1 - \lambda) \frac {L _ {p f}}{v _ {x}}.\tag{2}
$$

The preview driver model based on a torque input can be written as follows:

$$
\tau_ {h} = K _ {y} \big [ \lambda e _ {y n} + (1 - \lambda) e _ {y f} \big ].\tag{3}
$$

Here, $\tau _ { h }$ is the driver’s steering torque, and $K _ { y }$ is the gain coefficient of the driver’s steering torque. The driver model, as shown in (3), describes the relationship between the driver’s steering torque and varying preview characteristics [27].

## B. Parameters Identification of Driver Model

Four representative drivers with different driving styles were selected for identification experiments of driver time-varying parameters to characterize the actual preview characteristics of drivers in selected road scenarios. We used the HIL driving simulator and the simulation software CarSim to obtain pre-view deviations $e _ { y f }$ and $e _ { y n }$ at the near and far preview points, respectively. The preview deviation at the driver’s actual pre-view point was obtained by weighting the preview deviation at the near and far preview points. The road scenario is shown in Fig. 2. The longitudinal speed was set as $\nu _ { x } = 2 0$ m/s, and the near and far preview distances were set as 12 and 45 m, respectively.

Remark $I ;$ The measured data include the driver’s input steering torque $\tau _ { h } ,$ and lateral tracking deviations $e _ { y n }$ and $e _ { y f } .$ $\tau _ { h }$ is acquired using a Hella torque sensor. In the HIL driving simulator, the driver’s near and far points were set to a fixed value. Therefore, the lateral tracking deviations $e _ { y n }$ and $e _ { y f }$ can be obtained directly from the driving simulation software of the HIL test platform.

The measured values of $\tau _ { h } ,   e _ { y n } ,$ , and $e _ { y f }$ are shown in Figs. 3 and 4. They were used to identify parameters λ and $K _ { y }$ of the driver model using the recursive least squares method based on genetic factors. We used the window function $T _ { w } = 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { s }$ and regarded the test time $T$ as a finite component $n _ { \nu } .$ Assuming that the time-varying parameters are continuous in each time window, the performance indicator function can be expressed as follows:

$$
J = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n _ {v}} \frac {1}{T _ {w}} \int_ {(i - 1) T _ {w}} ^ {i T _ {w}} \zeta^ {n _ {v} - i} \left\{K _ {y} \left[ \lambda e _ {y n} + (1 - \lambda) e _ {y f} \right] - \tau_ {h} \right\} ^ {2} d t.\tag{4}
$$

Here, $\tau _ { h }$ is the driver’s input torque and $\zeta$ is the genetic factor $( 0 \prec \zeta \leq 1 )$ . To facilitate calculation, we define $K _ { \mathrm { y } } =$ $a _ { L } + b _ { L } ,   \lambda = a _ { L } / ( a _ { L } + b _ { L } )$ , and the performance index (4) as follows:

$$
\min _ {a _ {L}, b _ {L}} J = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n _ {v}} \frac {1}{T _ {w}} \int_ {(i - 1) T _ {w}} ^ {i T _ {w}} \zeta^ {n _ {v} - i} \left\{a _ {L} e _ {\mathrm{yn}} + b _ {L} e _ {\mathrm{yf}} - \tau_ {h} \right\} ^ {2} d t.\tag{5}
$$

Subsequently, we transform the driver model (3) into the standard least squares format, as follows:

$$
y (k) = \varphi^ {T} (k) \theta .\tag{6}
$$

Here, $\varphi ( k )$ is the data vector, and $\theta$ is the parameter vector to be evaluated

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \varphi (k) = \left[ e _ {y n} (k - 1), \dots , e _ {y n} (k - n _ {v}), e _ {\mathrm{yf}} (k - 1), \dots , e _ {\mathrm{yf}} (k - n _ {v}) \right] ^ {T} \\ \theta = \left[ a _ {L 1}, \dots , a _ {L n _ {v}}, b _ {L 1}, \dots , b _ {L n _ {v}} \right] ^ {T}. \end{array} \right.
$$

According to the least squares method based on genetic factors, the genetic factor of system parameters can be obtained to derive the least squares estimation of θ as follows:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \theta (k) = \theta (k - 1) + K (k) \big [ y (k) - \varphi^ {T} (k) \theta (k - 1) \big ] \\ K (k) = \frac {P (k - 1) \varphi (k)}{\lambda + \varphi^ {T} (k) P (k - 1) \varphi (k)} \\ P (k) = \frac {1}{\lambda} \big [ I - K (k) \varphi^ {T} (k) \big ] P (k - 1). \end{array} \right.
$$

Consequently, $P ( k ) = ( \Phi _ { k } ^ { T } \Phi _ { k } ) ^ { - 1 } ,   \Phi = [ \varphi ^ { T } ( 1 ) ,   \varphi ^ { T } ( 2 ) ,$ $\varphi ^ { T } ( n _ { \nu } ) ] ^ { T }$ , and the initial values were set as $\theta ( 0 )   =   0$ and $P ( 0 ) \; = \; \upsilon I$ , in which $\upsilon   =   1 0 ^ { 6 }$ , and I is the unit diagonal matrix.

Based on the driving data of four drivers, the relationship between preview time and curvature was obtained via the parameter identification method above, as shown in Fig. 5. Table I shows the identified parameters $a _ { 0 } , a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } ,$ and $K _ { y } .$ The results show that the driver’s preview time generally decreases with the increase in curvature because the driver is attempting to achieve a balance between track tracking accuracy and vehicle stability.

Remark 2: The driver’s steering gain coefficient $K _ { y }$ affects the amplitude of the driver’s steering torque. Table I shows that the identified parameter $K _ { y }$ can be considered a fixed value. The relationship between the identified preview time $t _ { p }$ and road curvature $\rho$ was fitted using the quadratic polynomial curve as expressed in (7).

The relationship between the curvature $\rho$ of road and the preview time $t _ { p }$ was obtained as follows:

$$
t _ {p} = a _ {2} | \rho | ^ {2} + a _ {1} | \rho | + a _ {0}\tag{7}
$$

$$
\lambda (\rho) = \frac {v _ {x}}{L _ {p n} - L _ {p f}} t _ {p} (\rho) - \frac {L _ {p f}}{L _ {p n} - L _ {p f}}.\tag{8}
$$

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 6. Steering-system model.

Here, $a _ { 0 } ,   a _ { 1 }$ , and $a _ { 2 }$ are polynomial coefficients. Therefore, the time-varying driver model with a change in road curvature can be obtained as follows:

$$
\tau_ {h} = K _ {y} \big [ \lambda (\rho) e _ {y n} + (1 - \lambda (\rho)) e _ {y f} \big ].\tag{9}
$$

The proposed varying preview driver model accurately describes the relationship between the road curvature $\rho$ and previewing time $t _ { p 1 }$

## III. VARYING PARAMETER HUMAN–VEHICLE–ROAD MODEL FOR HUMAN–MACHINE COOPERATION

## A. Steering-System Model

Currently, intelligent driving is primarily based on the steering angle control of an electric power steering system shown in Fig. 6, and the driver cannot intervene in the steering control, which results in the driver’s disengagement from the vehicle control. The dynamics of the steering system with a torque input for realizing the human–machine steering interaction is expressed as follows:

$$
J _ {e q} \ddot {\theta} _ {s w} + B _ {e q} \dot {\theta} _ {s w} + K _ {f z} \theta_ {s w} + \tau_ {\mathrm{dis}} = \tau_ {h} + \tau_ {m}.\tag{10}
$$

$J _ { e q }$ is the equivalent moment of inertia of the kingpin, $B _ { e q }$ is the equivalent damping of the kingpin, $K _ { f z }$ is the equivalent steering stiffness, $\theta _ { s w }$ is the steering wheel angle, $\tau _ { m }$ is the torque input of the intelligent driving system, and $\tau _ { \mathrm { d i s } }$ is the equivalent steering resistance torque. By combining (9) and (10), the steering-system model with driver input expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} J _ {e q} \ddot {\theta} _ {s w} + B _ {e q} \dot {\theta} _ {s w} + K _ {f z} \theta_ {s w} - K _ {y} \left[ \lambda (\rho) e _ {y n} + (1 - \lambda (\rho)) e _ {y f} \right] \\ + \tau_ {\mathrm{dis}} = \tau_ {m}. \end{array} \tag {11}
$$

## B. Vehicle Model

In this study, the classical vehicle model with two DOFs, as shown in Fig. 7, was adopted to represent the dynamics of the vehicle [28]. The dynamics model is expressed as follows:

$$
\dot {\beta} = a _ {1 1} \beta + a _ {1 2} \dot {\psi} + b _ {1} \theta_ {s w}\tag{12}
$$

$$
\ddot {\psi} = a _ {2 1} \beta + a _ {2 2} \dot {\psi} + b _ {2} \theta_ {s w}\tag{13}
$$

$$
\Delta \dot {\psi} = \dot {\psi} - v _ {x} \rho\tag{14}
$$

$$
\dot {e} _ {y} = v _ {y} \cos (\Delta \psi) + v _ {x} \sin (\Delta \psi)\tag{15}
$$

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 7. Two-DOF vehicle model.

$$
\dot {e} _ {y p} = \dot {e} _ {y} + v _ {x} t _ {p} (\rho) \frac {d [ \tan (\Delta \psi) ]}{d t}.\tag{16}
$$

$\beta$ is the lateral slip angle of the center of mass, $\nu _ { y }$ is the lateral velocity, and $\dot { \psi }$ is the yaw velocity. The other parameters are defined as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} a _ {1 1} = \frac {C _ {f} + C _ {r}}{m v _ {x}}, a _ {1 2} = \frac {l _ {f} C _ {f} - l _ {r} C _ {r}}{m v _ {x} ^ {2}}, a _ {2 1} = \frac {l _ {f} C _ {f} - l _ {r} C _ {r}}{I _ {z}} \\ a _ {2 2} = \frac {l _ {f} ^ {2} C _ {f} + l _ {r} ^ {2} C _ {r}}{I _ {z} v _ {x}}, b _ {1} = - \frac {C _ {f}}{m v _ {x} N _ {s}}, b _ {2} = - \frac {l _ {f} C _ {f}}{I _ {z} N _ {s}}. \end{array}
$$

## C. Varying Parameter Human–Vehicle–Road Model

A weight function of auxiliary output torque was introduced to solve the problem of man–machine control allocation [29], [30]. In [31], a varying parameter was introduced to strengthen or weaken the braking intervention degree, which can solve the coordination problem between the active front steering and braking system. The control input of the system was successfully weighted by introducing adjustment parameters.

Inspired by the results presented in [29]–[31], the penalty factor κ was introduced to the human–vehicle–road model, which can strengthen or weaken an autonomous assist input by assessing the consistency degree of human–machine driving intention to reduce human–machine conflicts.

To reduce human–machine conflicts and the mismatch in driving characteristics between a human and autonomous driving system, a linear variable parameter model (17) with the driver’s preview time $t _ { p }$ and penalty factor κ as variable parameters was established.

Combining (11)–(16), the varying parameter human– vehicle–road model is can be obtained as follows:

$$
\dot {x} = A x + B _ {1} w + B _ {2} u\tag{17}
$$

$$
z = C _ {1} x + D _ {1} w + D _ {2} u\tag{18}
$$

where

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c c c c} 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ - \frac {K _ {f z}}{J _ {e q}} & - \frac {B _ {e q}}{J _ {e q}} & 0 & 0 & K _ {y} & 0 \\ b _ {1} & 0 & a _ {1 1} & a _ {1 2} & 0 & 0 \\ b _ {2} & 0 & a _ {2 1} & a _ {2 2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & v _ {x} & v _ {x} t _ {p} (\rho) & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right]
$$

## A. Construction of Penalty Factor Based on Fuzzy Rules

The goal of cooperative driving control in this study is to mitigate steering conflicts between a human and a machine. When the driver is in the normal state, the intensity of the steering auxiliary torque should be reduced; meanwhile, when the driver is distracted, the steering auxiliary torque should be increased.

TABLE III FUZZY RULES

| $\tau_h$$e_{vp}$ | FD | FZ | L | ZZ | ZD |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FD | D | Z | L | Z | ZD |
| FZ | D | X | L | X | ZD |
| L | D | X | X | X | D |
| ZZ | ZD | X | L | X | D |
| ZD | ZD | Z | L | Z | D |

However, a penalty factor κ for human–machine intervention that can strengthen or weaken the autonomous assist input should be established to distribute the driving control rights such that human–machine conflicts are reduced. The consistency degree of the human–machine driving intention can be assessed based on the driver’s steering torque $\tau _ { h }$ and the changing trends of the lateral displacement offset $e _ { y p }$ at the preview point. Based on fuzzy theory, 25 fuzzy rules were formulated based on the offset $e _ { y p }$ of the driver’s preview point and the driver’s steering moment $\tau _ { h } ,$ , which can reflect the driver’s driving intention more completely. Consequently, the penalty factor κ of human–machine intervention can be determined to alleviate human–machine conflicts.

The inputs of the fuzzy controller are the offset of the pre-view point and the driver’s steering torque, and the output is the penalty factor. Among them, the range of is $[ - 0 . 4 ,   0 . 4 ]$ and the range of $\tau _ { h }$ is [−6, 6]. If the actual and values are outside the ranges above, then they are regarded as the boundary values of the range. The fuzzy subsets of $e _ { y p }$ and $\tau _ { h }$ are FD, $\mathrm { F Z ,   L ,   Z Z , }$ and $\mathbf { Z } \mathbf { D } ,$ which represent the five states of a negative large, negative medium, zero, and center and square of the offset and driver torque, respectively. The range of the penalty factor for the human–machine intervention is [0, 1]. The fuzzy subsets of L, X, Z, ZD, and D represent the five states of zero, small, medium, large, and large, respectively. The 3-D relationship among the offset, driver steering torque and assistance gain, and the three fuzzy membership functions are shown in Fig. 8.

The fuzzy rules are shown in Table III.

The typical rules are defined as follows.

1) If the vehicle’s offset $e _ { y p }$ is in the state of FD, and the driver’s steering torque $\tau _ { h }$ is in the state of FD, then the vehicle deviates significantly to the left from the lane, and the driver’s left turn operation exacerbates the vehicle deviation. The penalty factor κ is set as D for this scenario, which implies that the machine’s intervention is intensified to correct the vehicle deviation caused by the driver’s misoperation.

2) When the offset $e _ { y p }$ of the preview point is zero and the driver’s steering torque $\tau _ { h }$ is in the state of L, the vehicle is in the normal state of straight driving. In this scenario, the penalty factor κ is X, and a low assistance torque strength is applied to maintain the straight traversal of the vehicle.

3) When the offset $e _ { y p }$ and the driver’s steering torque $\tau _ { h }$ are both in the ZD state, the vehicle deviates significantly to the right of the lane, and the driver’s right turn, which is a result of misoperation, exacerbates the vehicle deviation. In this scenario, the output penalty factor κ is D, which implies that the machine’s intervention is intensified to correct the vehicle deviation.

Remark 4: The penalty factor κ is designed based on fuzzy rules. When a vehicle deviates from the lane and the driver’s misoperation intensifies the deviation, a larger penalty factor is output to promptly correct the vehicle deviation; however, when a vehicle deviates only slightly and the driver is correcting the deviation, the penalty factor is appropriately reduced to alleviate the driver’s discomfort arising from the excessive control of the machine system.

## B. Gain-Scheduling/LPV $H _ { \infty }$ Steering Torque Control Strategies for Human–Machine Co-Driving

Inspired by the study presented in [32], which considered multiple targets, including the path tracking error, system stability, and control output, we define the performance indicator function of human–machine cooperative steering torque control as follows:

$$
J = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \Big (q _ {1} e _ {y p} ^ {2} + q _ {2} \triangle \psi^ {2} + R u ^ {2} \Big) d t.\tag{19}
$$

Here, $q _ { 1 } ,   q _ { 2 }$ , and $R$ are weight coefficients, and $z = C _ { 1 } x +$ $D_{1}w  +  D_{2}u$ can be obtained using (18). The performance index shown in (19) can be rewritten as follows:

$$
J = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \bigl ((C _ {1} X + D _ {1} w) ^ {T} Q (C _ {1} X + D _ {1} w) + (D _ {2} u) ^ {T} R (D _ {2} u) \bigr) d t\tag{20}
$$

where, $\mathcal { Q } = \left[ \begin{matrix} { q _ { 1 } } & { 0 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { q _ { 2 } } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } & { 0 } \end{matrix} \right] .$

The performance index function shown in (20) can be rewritten as follows:

$$
J = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \binom{\left(Q ^ {1 / 2} C _ {1} X + Q ^ {1 / 2} D _ {1} w\right) ^ {T} \left(Q ^ {1 / 2} C _ {1} X + Q ^ {1 / 2} D _ {1} w\right)}{+ \left(R ^ {1 / 2} D _ {2} u\right) ^ {T} \left(R ^ {1 / 2} D _ {2} u\right)} d t.\tag{21}
$$

Based on the performance index, the auxiliary evaluation signal of human–machine cooperative H∞ $H _ { \infty }$ control is defined

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 9. Polytope of preview time and penalty factor.

as follows:

$$
z _ {0} = Q ^ {1 / 2} C _ {1} X + Q ^ {1 / 2} D _ {1} w + R ^ {1 / 2} D _ {2} u.\tag{22}
$$

Subsequently, combining (17) and (22), the system state equation can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \dot {x} = A (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) x + B _ {1} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) w + B _ {2} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) u \\ z _ {0} = Q ^ {1 / 2} C _ {1} x + Q ^ {1 / 2} D _ {1} w + R ^ {1 / 2} D _ {2} u. \end{array}\tag{23}
$$

Based on robust $H _ { \infty }$ control theory, if an arbitrarily small positive $\gamma$ exists, then the transfer function $T _ { z _ { 0 } \omega }$ from the disturbance w to the auxiliary output $x _ { 0 }$ should satisfy $\| T _ { z _ { 0 } \omega } \| _ { \infty } = \operatorname { \mathfrak { s u p } } _ { ( w \neq 0 ) } \| z _ { 0 } \| _ { 2 } / \| w \| _ { 2 } \prec \gamma .$ Subsequently, the control input u can be obtained using this formula. The appropriate control input u can be specified such that $\| T _ { z _ { 0 } \omega } \| _ { \infty } = \operatorname { s u p } _ { ( w \neq 0 ) } \| z _ { 0 } \| _ { 2 } / \| w \| _ { 2 } \prec \gamma$ holds, which results in a stable system and a suboptimal performance index under the disturbance w [33].

Herein, we select $t _ { p }$ and κ as varying parameters and denote $\boldsymbol { \xi } = [ t _ { p } , \kappa ] ^ { T }$ , where

$$
\left| t _ {p} \in [ t _ {p} \quad \overline {{t _ {p}}} ],   \kappa \in [ \underline {{\kappa}} \quad \bar {\kappa} ] \right|.
$$

Here, $\begin{aligned}& \text{" } \underline{\quad} \text{" } \\& \underline{\quad} \underline{\quad}\end{aligned}$ and $\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned}\\ & \text{" } \text{" } \\& \text{" } \text{" }\\ &\end{aligned}\\ \end{aligned}$ represent the minimum and maximum values, respectively.

For the LPV system, if the closed-loop stability can be guaranteed in the entire varying-parameter trajectory, then the entire system can be regarded as stable. However, the stability of the entire trajectory is difficult to guarantee when varying parameters are involved [34], [35]. If the LPV system exhibits a polytopic structure, then its stability can be guaranteed by the stabilities of polytopic vertices [36]. Hence, the variable parameters were described based on polytopic vertices [37]–[39]. The system used in this study is a polytopic LPV system with vertices M, N, O, and P, as shown in Fig. 9.

Next, the following parameter-dependent control law is considered:

$$
u = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {4} \eta_ {j} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) K _ {j} x = K (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) x, \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {4} \eta_ {j} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) = 1.\tag{24}
$$

The control goal is to design the feedback gains $K _ { j } ,$ where $j \in \{ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 \}$

Subsequently, $\eta _ { j } ( \boldsymbol { \xi } )$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\eta_ {1} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) = \frac {\left| \underline {{\zeta}} _ {1} - \zeta_ {1} \right|}{\bar {\zeta} _ {1} - \underline {{\zeta}} _ {1}} \cdot \frac {\left| \underline {{\zeta}} _ {2} - \zeta_ {2} \right|}{\bar {\zeta} _ {2} - \underline {{\zeta}} _ {2}}, \eta_ {2} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) = \frac {\left| \underline {{\zeta}} _ {1} - \zeta_ {1} \right|}{\bar {\zeta} _ {1} - \underline {{\zeta}} _ {1}} \cdot \frac {\left| \bar {\zeta} - \zeta_ {2} \right|}{\bar {\zeta} _ {2} - \underline {{\zeta}} _ {2}}
$$

$$
\eta_ {3} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) = \frac {| \bar {\zeta} - \zeta_ {1} |}{\bar {\zeta} _ {1} - \underline {{\zeta}} _ {1}} \cdot \frac {| \underline {{\zeta}} _ {2} - \zeta_ {2} |}{\bar {\zeta} _ {2} - \underline {{\zeta}} _ {2}}, \eta_ {4} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) = \frac {| \bar {\zeta} - \zeta_ {1} |}{\bar {\zeta} _ {1} - \underline {{\zeta}} _ {1}} \cdot \frac {| \bar {\zeta} _ {2} - \zeta_ {2} |}{\bar {\zeta} _ {2} - \underline {{\zeta}} _ {2}}.
$$

Combining the above with (21), the closed-loop control LPV system can be expressed as follows:

$$
\boxed {\left\{ \begin{array}{l} \dot {x} = A _ {c l} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) x + B _ {1} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) w \\ z _ {0} = C _ {c l} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) x + D _ {3} w. \end{array} \right.}\tag{25}
$$

Here, $A _ { c l } ( \pmb { \xi } ) \; = \; A ( \pmb { \xi } )   +   B _ { 2 } ( \pmb { \xi } ) K ( \pmb { \xi } ) , C _ { c l } ( \pmb { \xi } ) \; = \; \mathcal { Q } ^ { 1 / 2 } C _ { 1 } \; +$ $R ^ { 1 / 2 } D _ { 2 } K ( \xi )$ , and $D _ { 3 } = Q ^ { 1 / 2 } D _ { 1 }$

To ensure the stability of the system under the effects of <sup>τ</sup>dis and $\rho ,$ the robust stability condition is introduced to the system (25), as described in Lemmas 1 and 2.

Lemma 1 (Apkarian et al. [35]): A closed-loop LPV system (25) can be obtained for a controller $K ( \xi )$ . For this system, the following propositions are equivalent.

1) A positive-definite solution X exists for all $( A _ { c l } ( \pmb { \xi } ) , B _ { 1 } ( \pmb { \xi } ) , C _ { c l } ( \pmb { \xi } ) , D _ { 3 } )$ , such that

$$
\Gamma (K (\boldsymbol {\zeta}), X, \gamma) = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} A _ {c l} ^ {T} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) X + X A _ {c l} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) & X B _ {1} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) & C _ {c l} ^ {T} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) \\ B _ {1} ^ {T} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) X & - \gamma I & D _ {3} ^ {T} \\ C _ {c l} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) & D _ {3} & - \gamma I \end{array} \right] \prec 0.\tag{26}
$$

2) The closed-loop LPV system (25) is stable and exhibits quadratic $H _ { \infty }$ performance γ for all possible parameter trajectories ζ . Mathematically

$$
\left\| T _ {z _ {0} \omega} \right\| _ {\infty} = \sup _ {(w \neq 0)} \| z _ {0} \| _ {2} / \| w \| _ {2} \prec \gamma\tag{27}
$$

where $T _ { z _ { 0 } \omega }$ is the transfer function from the disturbance w to the auxiliary output $z _ { 0 } .$ Lemma 1 can be obtained by constructing an appropriate Lyapunov function, such as $V ( \pmb { \zeta } ) = \pmb { x } ^ { T } \pmb { X } \pmb { x } ,$ in addition to the necessary numerical operations.

To guarantee dynamic performance and stability, the poles of the system (25) should be specified within a certain range. The closed-loop system (25) is a polytopic LPV system; therefore, the D-stability condition can be used to guarantee stability. To ensure that the dynamic system exhibits the minimum attenuation $\alpha ,$ the minimum damping factor $\xi   =   \cos \sigma$ , and the maximum natural frequency $\omega _ { 0 } = r \mathrm { s i n } \sigma$ , the closed-loop pole assignment area should be restricted in the region $D ( \alpha , r , \sigma )$ Next, Lemma 2 is introduced.

Lemma 2 (Toulotte et al. $[ 4 0 ] ) { : }$ For a specified LMI region $D ( \alpha , r , \sigma )$ and matrix $A _ { c l }   \in   R ^ { n \times n }$ in the complex plane, the matrix $A _ { c l }$ is stable if all the eigenvalues of matrix $A _ { c l }$ are in region $D ( \alpha , r , \sigma )$ . For all the poles of matrix $A _ { c l }$ to be in region $D ( \alpha , r , \sigma )$ , a positive-definite matrix X satisfying (28)–(30) must exist

$$
\Omega^ {\alpha} (K, X) = A _ {c l} X + X A _ {c l} ^ {T} + 2 \alpha X \prec 0\tag{28}
$$

$$
\Omega^ {r} (K, X) = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} - r X & A _ {c l} X \\ X A _ {c l} ^ {T} & - r X \end{array} \right] \prec 0\tag{29}
$$

$$
\Omega^ {\sigma} (K, X) = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \left(A _ {c l} X + X A _ {c l} ^ {T}\right) \sin \sigma & \left(A _ {c l} X - X A _ {c l} ^ {T}\right) \cos \sigma \\ \left(X A _ {c l} ^ {T} - A _ {c l} X\right) \cos \sigma & \left(X A _ {c l} ^ {T} + A _ {c l} X\right) \sin \sigma \end{array} \right]\tag{\( \prec 0. \}
$$

(30)

However, because of variable parameters $t _ { p }$ and κ of the human–vehicle–road model, the corresponding control strategy could not be derived using the conditions stipulated in Lemmas 1 and 2. For brevity, we assume that the variations of the driver parameters are bounded by the following:

$$
\boldsymbol {\zeta} = [ \zeta_ {1}, \zeta_ {2} ] ^ {T}, \zeta_ {1} = t _ {p} \in \left[ \begin{array}{c c} t _ {\underline {{p}}} & \overline {{t _ {p}}} \end{array} \right], \zeta_ {2} = \kappa \in \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \underline {{\kappa}} & \bar {\kappa} \end{array} \right].
$$

Using the boundaries defined above, the closed-loop system can be represented by the matrix set $\Sigma _ { i } \quad : =$ $\left( A_{cli} \quad B_{1i} \quad C_{cli} \quad D_{3} \right)$ , where $i \in \{ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 \}$

The coefficient matrixes at the four vertices of the polytope, as shown in Fig. 9, can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Sigma_ {1} := \left( \begin{array}{c c} A _ {c l} (\underline {{\zeta}} _ {1}, \underline {{\zeta}} _ {2}) & B _ {1} (\underline {{\zeta}} _ {1}) \\ C _ {c l} (\underline {{\zeta}} _ {1}, \underline {{\zeta}} _ {2}) & D _ {3} \end{array} \right), \Sigma_ {2} := \left( \begin{array}{c c} A _ {c l} (\underline {{\zeta}} _ {1}, \bar {\zeta} _ {2}) & B _ {1} (\underline {{\zeta}} _ {1}) \\ C _ {c l} (\underline {{\zeta}} _ {1}, \bar {\zeta}) & D _ {3} \end{array} \right) \\ \Sigma_ {3} := \left( \begin{array}{c c} A _ {c l} \big (\bar {\zeta} _ {1}, \underline {{\zeta}} _ {2} \big) & B _ {1} \big (\bar {\zeta} _ {1} \big) \\ C _ {c l} \big (\bar {\zeta} _ {1}, \underline {{\zeta}} _ {2} \big) \big) & D _ {3} \end{array} \right), \Sigma_ {4} := \left( \begin{array}{c c} A _ {c l} \big (\bar {\zeta} _ {1}, \bar {\zeta} _ {2} \big) & B _ {1} \big (\bar {\zeta} _ {1} \big) \\ C _ {c l} \big (\bar {\zeta} _ {1}, \bar {\zeta} \big) & D _ {3} \end{array} \right) \end{array}\tag{31}
$$

The feedback control strategy $u \; = \; K ( \pmb { \zeta } ) x$ can be transformed into a convex composite system (26), which guarantees the stability and tracking performance in the parameters’ range of MNOP.

The $H _ { \infty }$ solution of gain scheduling for the human–machine co-driving linear variable parameter system can be obtained from Corollary 1.

Corollary 1: If the system (25) contains a feedback gain matrix $K _ { j }$ at all four vertices of the multicellular MNOP, then a positive-definite matrix X and a robust control performance parameter $\gamma > 0$ exist. Therefore

$$
\begin{array}{c} \Gamma_ {j} \big (K _ {j}, X, \gamma \big) \prec 0, j \in \{1, 2, 3, 4 \} \\ \Omega_ {j} ^ {\Xi} \big (K _ {j}, X \big) \prec 0, j \in \{1, 2, 3, 4 \} \text {and} \Xi \in \{\alpha , \gamma , \sigma \}. \end{array}\tag{32}
$$

(33)

Proof: The time-varying system (25) is applicable at any working point $( \zeta _ { 1 } , \zeta _ { 2 } )$ . The time-varying system (25) can be written as follows:

$$
\Gamma_ {(\boldsymbol {\zeta})} (K (\boldsymbol {\zeta}), X, \gamma) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {4} \left[ \eta_ {j} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) \Gamma_ {j} \big (K _ {j}, X, \gamma \big) \right]\tag{34}
$$

$$
\Omega_ {(\zeta)} ^ {\Xi} (K (\boldsymbol {\zeta}), X) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {4} \bigl [ \eta_ {j} (\boldsymbol {\zeta}) \Omega_ {j} \bigl (K _ {j}, X \bigr) \bigr ].\tag{35}
$$

Because of $\eta _ { j } ( \zeta ) \succ 0 ,$ , and by the inequalities presented in (32) and (33), the following inequality is established:

$$
\Gamma_ {(\boldsymbol {\zeta})} (K (\boldsymbol {\zeta}), X, \gamma) \prec 0\tag{36}
$$

$$
\Omega_ {(\zeta)} ^ {\Xi} (K (\zeta), X) \prec 0.\tag{37}
$$

Therefore, using Lemma 1 and (36), the state-feedback gain $K ( \xi )$ and Lyapunov functions can guarantee the asymptotic stability of the time-varying system (25). Using Lemma 2 and (37), the working point $( \zeta _ { 1 } , \zeta _ { 2 } )$ of the time-varying system (25) is constrained within a certain region by the statefeedback matrix $K ( \xi )$ , which effectively ensures the control performance of the human–machine system.

The LMI method can be used to solve X and $K _ { j }$ by multiplying $( X ^ { - 1 } , I , I )$ on both sides of the $\Gamma _ { j } ( K _ { j } , X , \gamma ) ;$

subsequently, (26) can be converted to solve the LMIs

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c c c} A _ {i} P + P A _ {i} ^ {T} + W _ {j} ^ {T} B _ {2 i} ^ {T} + B _ {2 i} W _ {j} & B _ {1 i} ^ {T} & P C _ {1} ^ {T} + W _ {j} ^ {T} D _ {2} ^ {T} \\ B _ {1 i} & - \gamma I & D _ {3} ^ {T} \\ P C _ {1} + W _ {j} D _ {2} & D _ {3} & - \gamma I \end{array} \right] \prec 0 i, j \in \{1, 2, 3, 4 \}. \tag {3}\tag{38}
$$

By substituting $P = X ^ { - 1 }$ and $W _ { j } = K _ { j } P ,$ the solution X and feedback gain $K _ { j }$ of the Lyapunov function can be obtained.

By limiting the closed-loop pole positions, the stability and performance of the human–machine steering torque control strategy are guaranteed. Fig. 10 shows the position of the system poles. The blue contour lines represent the constraint areas, where $\text{" } \mathbf{0} \text{" }$ and “\*” represent the pole positions of the open-loop and closed-loop systems [(17) and (25), respectively], respectively. The pole location map shows that all the closed-loop poles can be restricted to a certain region.

Remark 5: By applying the gain-scheduling control strategy, human–machine cooperative steering control was achieved by adjusting the preview time and penalty factor of human– machine intervention, and human–machine steering conflicts were alleviated. The stability and performance of the control can be guaranteed in the entire range of the variable parameters.

## V. SIMULATION AND RESULTS

The LMI and LPV methods were simulated at a constant speed of 72 km/h under a multicurvature serpentine path. In the LPV control, the preview characteristic was set the same as that for the first participant, and the penalty factor was 1, which implies that the control authority is completely transferred to the LPV controller without the intervention of human drivers. In the LMI control, the preview time was set as 0.95 s for comparison. Compared with the LMI control, the LPV control exhibits the characteristics of human-like time-varying previews.

As shown in Fig. 11(a), the LPV controller exhibits good track tracking capabilities. When entering the curve at approximately 12 s, the LMI control exhibits control overshoot owing to the interference of the curve. The LPV controller can reduce the oscillation of the vehicle trajectory by limiting the system poles. A comparison of the steering control torque is shown in Fig. 11(b). The LMI control lags at 12 s and requires a large torque to complete path tracking. Compared with the LMI controller, the LPV controller requires a much smaller torque and can achieve accurate trajectory tracking with less torque intervention.

Fig. 11(c) and (d) shows results of the yaw rate and sideslip angle, respectively. The yaw rate and sideslip angle are important indices for evaluating vehicle stability. As shown in Fig. 11(c) and (d), the overshoot of the yaw rate and sideslip angle controlled by the LPV controller is significantly less than that controlled by the LMI, respectively, and the size is within the safety range, which ensures the stability of the vehicle. The LPV controller exhibits high anti-interference capability and system robustness, which can improve tracking performance while ensuring driving stability.

## VI. TEST AND RESULTS

An illustration of the HIL experimental platform is shown in Fig. 12. NI-PXI is embedded with the CarSim real-time simulation environment to execute the high-fidelity vehicle model and road model. The driver generates the steering torque τh based on the visual feedback of the real-time driving scene and the road sense feedback. As the steering controller of the automatic driving system, MicroAutobox performs the man– machine co-driving steering control strategy in real time to calculate the target steering torque $\tau _ { m }$ and controls the motor to output the steering moment through the motor drive circuit. The driver and autopilot system simultaneously exert a torque to the steering actuator, thereby completing the lane-keeping task through cooperation.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 13. Results of HIL experiments without driver intervention. (a) Lateral displacement. (b) Steering torque.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 14. Comparisons of lateral displacement in co-driving HIL tests.

The classic large curvature serpentine path was established, and the longitudinal speed was set to 60 km/h. Prior to performing the HIL experiments of human–machine co-driving, the human-like driving characteristics, high robustness, and good path tracking the performance of the proposed controller must be ensured. To perform the automatic steering test without the driver’s intervention, one among three methods can be considered: 1) LPV control; 2) LMI control; and 3) NO SAS. LPV control and LMI control have been introduced in the preceding section. In NO SAS, the first participant tracks the entire path in the simulated driver without any SAS.

The results of the HIL experiments without driver intervention are shown in Fig. 13. The lateral displacement and steering torque suggest that the three types of driving schemes can effectively realize the path-following effect; however, the LMI control strategy from the first corner exhibits a considerable lag as compared with the other control strategies. Hence, the LMI control strategy differs significantly from the steering characteristics of human drivers. The LPV controller with time-varying preview characteristics is highly similar to the steering behavior of human drivers.

To further verify the control effect of the designed LPV human–machine cooperative controller, we performed human– machine co-driving experiments. Four representative drivers were required in the HIL driving simulator to perform driving on the same road, and the driver and the LPV controller shared the driving control authority. Subsequently, LMI control and NO SAS were established.

The human–machine co-driving experiments of four drivers based on the LPV controller are shown in Figs. 14–16. The steering torque suggests that the driving characteristics of the four drivers are different. The first driver is accustomed to steering in advance in the corner, whereas the second and third drivers exhibit a slightly lower steering time, which may affect the accuracy of vehicle path tracking. At this moment, the human–machine co-driving controller is required to assist the steering action of the driver. Figs. 15 and 16 show that the LPV controller can assist the correction of the driver’s improper steering operation in a timely manner.

Fig. 17 shows the change process of the preview time and penalty factor in the human–machine intervention. The pre-view time varies with the curvature of the road. A larger preview time is maintained on a straight road, whereas a smaller preview time is maintained on a curved road with a larger curvature to ensure that the vehicle can pass promptly and safely, which is consistent with the driving characteristics of human drivers.

The penalty factor is changed to primarily increase or decrease the steering intervention intensity of the autonomous driving system such that the driver can maintain the straight traversal of the vehicle. The driver’s driving habits and psychology render it difficult for the driver to maintain good driving habits when crossing the curve continuously. Therefore, depending on the driver’s physical condition and the road condition, the controller increases the steering intervention intensity of the automatic driving system through the penalty factor, which reduces the driver’s tension and allows the vehicle to maintain a good track tracking performance.

Fig. 17. Variable parameters of the human–machine cooperative controller for different participants. (a) Participant 1. (b) Participant 2. (c) Participant 3. (d) Participant 4.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 18. Comparisons of RMS of steering torque of three control schemes.

In addition to LPV human–machine co-driving experiments, LMI co-driving control experiments with a fixed preview and the NO SAS scheme were performed. The RMS values of steering torque of the drivers for the three schemes, as shown in Fig. 18, were used to evaluate the physical load of the drivers. As shown in the figure, the average steering torque of drivers without the driver assistance intervention is approximately 1.5 times that of the drivers assisted by the LPV controller. Because the penalty factor for the human–machine intervention changes with time, the driver using the LPV controller expends less effort as compared with the driver using the LMI controller.

Fig. 19. Comparison of path tracking errors based on different participants. (a)–(d) Path tracking error/(m).

Fig. 19 shows the tracking errors of the three schemes based on a box diagram. Compared with the LMI and NO SAS schemes, the LPV co-driving scheme exhibits relatively small path tracking errors. In general, the path tracking errors are concentrated in a small range, and the proposed co-driving method can effectively correct errors and realize path tracking.

## VII. SUMMARY

In this study, a human–machine cooperative steering torque control was proposed. First, a time-varying preview driver model was constructed, and a penalty factor for human– machine intervention was established based on fuzzy rules to reduce human–machine steering conflicts. By applying gain-scheduling/LPV $H _ { \infty }$ control strategies, human–machine cooperative steering control was achieved by adjusting the penalty factor online. Finally, the proposed algorithm was verified via HIL experiments. The results demonstrated the human-like driving behavior of the proposed controller as well as its path tracking ability, which significantly reduced human– machine conflicts. The results presented herein are applicable to human–machine cooperative driving theory for achieving the desired driving safety, driving comfort, and autonomous driving system.

In the future, we will continue to analyze driver characteristics using advanced sensors to obtain driver data based on more scenarios such that more accurate and comprehensive driver characteristics can be obtained. To better illustrate the practicability of the control scheme, actual car experiments using the human–machine co-driving steering controller designed in this study will be performed for various road scenarios.
